Certification authority (CA)
Machine certificates, user certificates, SSL certificates... Oh, my! Clearly, you need to be familiar with
working with and deploying certificates to make use of AOVPN. This is becoming more and more
common with newer, well-secured technologies of any flavor. The major requirement here is that
you will need to have PKI inside your environment and at least one Windows CA server to issue the
necessary certificates. The following is a list of the places in which certificates could be used by an
AOVPN infrastructure:
• User certificates: These are the certificates issued to your VPN users from an internal CA, used
for authentication of the user tunnel.
• Machine certificates: These are certificates issued to your workstations (mostly laptops) from
an internal CA, used for authentication of the device tunnel.
• SSL certificates: These are installed on your Remote Access server to validate the incoming
traffic for SSTP VPN connections.
• VPN and NPS machine certificates: Your Remote Access server, as well as your NPS servers,
which we will talk about in just a minute, require machine certificates issued by your internal
CA.
Network Policy Server (NPS)
NPS is basically the authentication decision maker for VPN connections. When a VPN connection
request comes in, the Remote Access server hands that authentication request over to an NPS server
to validate who that user is, and also to verify that the user has permissions to log in via the VPN.
Most commonly, when working with Microsoft VPN connections, we configure NPS so that it allows
only users who are part of a certain Active Directory security group. For example, if you create a group
called VPN Users and then point NPS to that group, it will only allow users who you have placed inside
that group to make successful VPN connections.
NPS is another Windows Server role that can be hosted on its own system or spread across multiple
servers for redundancy. As with the Remote Access role, there is no Server 2025 requirement for NPS.
You could easily deploy it on previous versions of Windows Server just as well.
Keep in mind that you should not install NPS onto the same server where you are running Remote
Access. You need to spin up a second server for the purposes of NPS.

Unit Testing is the name given to a method of software testing that helps to
determine whether the isolated modules of a program (units) are working correctly.
After the various units have been verified, they can be merged together and tested as
a whole (integration testing and system testing) and/or released in production.
Given this definition, it's pretty easy to understand the importance of properly
defining and isolating the various units. These are the smallest testable parts of our
software, featuring a few inputs and a single output. In Object-Oriented
Programming (OOP), where the program's source code is split into classes, a unit is
often a method of a super, abstract, or derived class, yet it can also be a static
function of a helper class.
Although they've become a de facto standard for high-quality projects, unit tests are
often underestimated by most developers and project managers who are eager to
speed up the whole development process and therefore reduce its overall cost. Such
an approach may not be acceptable for small-scale projects with low-profit margins
since creating unit tests undeniably requires some additional work. However, it's
very important to understand their huge benefits for medium-to-big projects and
enterprise solutions, especially if they require the coordinated effort of a large
number of developers.

The `border-radius` properties replace each sharp border corner with an elliptical curve. One radius defines a circular corner, while separate horizontal and vertical radii define an ellipse.

The `box-shadow` property paints one or more shadows around an element's border box. Each shadow can specify horizontal and vertical offsets, blur radius, spread distance, color, and whether it is inset.

Comma-separated shadows are layered with the first shadow on top. Shadows are visual effects and do not alter layout dimensions, though they can extend beyond the box and overlap neighboring content.

This division suggests two styles of automation. Operator calls resemble actions a user performs and often depend on mode or selection, while direct datablock access names and changes data explicitly. Effective scripts combine both while remaining clear about which state each operation relies on.

Internally, `bpy.data` is created through the [[Blender Python RNA Bridge]]: Blender wraps its [[Blender Main Database]] in a [[Blender PointerRNA]] and then in a CPython extension object. Custom attribute functions route Python reads and writes through the RNA Data API instead of exposing raw DNA structures.

The `clear` property prevents a box from appearing beside earlier floats on selected sides. The browser moves the box downward until its relevant border edge is below the bottom margin edge of those floats.

Clearing acts on the element itself rather than canceling [[CSS Floats]]. It creates enough clearance for the box to avoid the specified float side while later content can still respond to remaining floats.

The `display` property controls the kind of box an element generates and the formatting role it adopts. Values can create block, inline, list-item, inline-block, table-related, flex, or grid behavior, and `none` suppresses box generation entirely.

The source also covers multi-keyword concepts such as outer flow and inner formatting roles. Changing display affects layout, not the document element's semantic identity.

Because this block travels with the serialized data, a reader does not need to assume that the file's C layouts match the running executable. Project templates establish the initial SDK and target framework configuration, while later commands operate from the project file's declared dependencies. Command help and template listings make the tool self-describing enough to discover available operations without an IDE-specific menu.

The `flex-basis` property establishes an item's starting main-axis size before [[CSS Flex Grow and Shrink|growth or shrinkage]] distributes free space. It can use a length, percentage, content-based value, or `auto` behavior that consults the relevant width or height.

A zero basis asks items to divide space mainly according to flex factors, whereas an automatic or content basis preserves more of their starting size. The `flex` shorthand combines basis, growth, and shrink factors.

The `flex-direction` property chooses the main axis and its forward direction. Row and row-reverse follow the inline axis, while column and column-reverse follow the block axis.

Because inline and block directions depend on [[CSS Writing Modes and Direction]], row does not universally mean left to right. Reverse values change visual placement but do not rewrite the document's source or reading order.

The `flex-grow` factor determines how positive free space is divided among flex items. A factor represents a proportion of the sum of growth factors, so items with larger factors receive more of the remaining space.

The `flex-shrink` factor participates when the line is too small. Shrinkage is scaled by both the factor and the item's flex base size, preventing a small item and a large item with equal factors from losing the same raw width.

The `flex-wrap` property decides whether flex items remain on one line or are divided across several lines when they do not fit. Wrapping can proceed in the normal cross-axis direction or in reverse.

Each flex line distributes its own free space, so items on different lines do not necessarily align to the same main-axis sizes. The `flex-flow` shorthand combines wrapping with [[CSS Flex Direction]].

The `font-size` property accepts absolute-size keywords, relative-size keywords, lengths, and percentages. Relative keywords and percentages are calculated from the inherited font size, while units such as `em` and `rem` refer to element or root font metrics.

Children inherit the computed font size rather than re-running the parent's original percentage expression. This prevents a percentage from compounding at every generation unless it is explicitly declared again.

The `font-style` property chooses among normal, italic, and oblique faces. Italic usually requests a separately designed face, whereas oblique requests a slanted presentation when that distinction is available.

The `font-stretch` property requests a condensed or expanded face along a named scale. Both properties participate in [[CSS Font Matching]], and `@font-face` descriptors state which style and stretch a downloaded resource supplies.

The `font-weight` property selects how light or bold a font face should appear. CSS accepts named values such as normal and bold, numeric weights from 100 through 900, and relative values that seek a bolder or lighter face than the inherited weight.

Available fonts may not supply every requested weight, so [[CSS Font Matching]] maps the request to a suitable face. An `@font-face` weight descriptor declares which requests a downloadable resource represents.

The `isolation` property can force an element to establish a separate stacking context for blending. Descendant blend modes then composite within that group instead of blending directly with content behind the isolated ancestor.

Isolation makes the blend backdrop predictable and prevents a local visual effect from interacting with unrelated page layers. The completed group can still be composited as one result into the surrounding scene.

The `justify-content` property distributes flex items along a flex line's main axis after flexible lengths and automatic margins have been resolved. Items can collect at the start, end, or center, or share remaining space between or around them.

The property controls leftover space rather than calculating each item's flexible base size. Its physical direction follows [[CSS Flex Direction]] and the writing mode.

The `line-height` property defines the minimum height of an inline box's line area and contributes to the height of each line box. Extra space beyond the font size is distributed as leading above and below the glyph area.

A unitless number scales with each element's own font size when inherited, whereas a computed length can pass unchanged to descendants. This distinction makes unitless line-height useful across text whose font sizes vary.

The `list-style-image` property replaces an ordinary list marker with an image when that image is available. The `list-style-position` property places the marker outside the principal block box or inside it as part of the content flow.

The `list-style` shorthand combines type, image, and position. A marker type can remain as a fallback when the image cannot be loaded.

The `list-style-type` property chooses the marker used by a list item. Values include bullets, numbers, alphabetic forms, and many language-specific systems, while `none` suppresses the marker.

The marker belongs to the list-item formatting model rather than to the document's text content. [[CSS Counters and Counter Styles]] supplies the numbering behavior behind many marker types and supports custom patterns.

The `Main` structure is Blender's central storehouse for loaded datablocks. It contains separate linked lists for scenes, objects, meshes, materials, images, cameras, worlds, actions, screens, window managers, and many other persistent categories.

Most ordinary [[Blender Blend File Block]] records ultimately become items in these lists. [[Blender LibBlock Linking]] restores their internal and cross-object pointers, and [[Blender Context Main Assignment]] installs the reconstructed database into the current [[Blender bContext Structure]].

The `makesrna` module defines and generates the infrastructure behind Blender RNA and the Data API. Unlike an ordinary runtime-only module, it contains code compiled into a generator as well as code compiled into the final Blender executable.

Its [[Blender RNA Definition API]] describes wrappers for DNA types, while its build-time process writes [[Blender RNA Generated Source]]. The `object-position` property aligns the fitted object within any remaining or clipped space. These properties change the external content inside the box without changing the box's own declared dimensions.

The `overflow` property determines what happens when content exceeds a box's available dimensions. It can remain visible, be clipped, or become accessible through a scrolling mechanism, and overflow behavior can create a clipping region around padding edges.

The `visibility` property hides painting while generally preserving the box's layout space. This differs from `display: none`, which suppresses box generation and causes surrounding layout to be recalculated without the element.

The `shape-outside` property defines the wrapping contour used around a floated element. It can name a reference box, use a basic shape such as a circle, ellipse, inset rectangle, or polygon, or derive a contour from image transparency.

The `text-align` property controls the inline-axis alignment of content within a block container. Values can align lines to a physical side, center them, justify them, or use start and end directions that follow the writing mode.

Alignment applies to inline content inside the block rather than moving the block box itself. `text-align-last` can separately control the final line of a block or a line immediately before a forced break.

The `text-indent` property offsets the first formatted line of a block container. The value can be positive or negative and may use a length or a percentage based on the containing block's width.

Indentation changes line layout without inserting characters into the document. A negative value can create a hanging indent, but the shifted text may require matching padding or margins to keep it from leaving the visible box.

The `text-shadow` property paints one or more shadows behind text. Each shadow supplies horizontal and vertical offsets, an optional blur radius, and an optional color; comma-separated shadows are layered together.

A zero-blur shadow produces a sharp displaced copy, while increasing blur softens its edge. Several shadows can create outlines or depth effects, but they do not alter the text's layout dimensions.

The `text-transform` property changes the displayed capitalization of text without changing the underlying document content. It can request uppercase, lowercase, capitalization, or no transformation.

Because the transformation is presentational, copied or otherwise processed content can retain its source spelling. The exact result of case conversion depends on the document language and the user agent's handling of language-specific rules.

The `transform-origin` property chooses the point around which an element is rotated, scaled, or otherwise transformed. Horizontal and vertical components can use keywords, lengths, or percentages, and a third length can place the origin along the z-axis.

The 12 factors are as follows:
1. Code base: One code base is tracked in revision control for many deployments.
2. Dependencies: Explicitly declare and isolate dependencies.
3. Config: Store config in the environment.
4. Backing services: Treat backing services as attached resources.

6. Processes: Execute the app as one or more stateless processes.
7. Port binding: Export services via port binding.
8. Concurrency: Scale out via the process model.
9. Disposability: Maximize robustness with fast startup and graceful shutdown.
10. Dev/prod parity: Keep development, staging, and production as similar as possible.
11. Logs: Treat logs as event streams.
12. Admin processes: Run admin/management tasks as one-off processes.

breaking them down into small, loosely coupled services that can be run in different environ -
ments and deployed on cloud-based platforms. You can learn more about this methodology at

Representing rotations in 3D is more complex than in 2D. Previously, an actor only needed

The addition property of equality states that adding equal quantities to equal quantities preserves equality. If (a=b), then for any real (c),

$$a+c=b+c.$$

Subtracting the same quantity from both sides is the same rule applied with an [[Opposite Number]]. It supports moving a term across an equation without changing the solution, provided the shorthand is understood as an operation on both sides. The property is central to producing [[Equivalent Equations]].

The addition property of inequality states that adding the same real number to both sides preserves their order. If (a<b), then

$$a+c<b+c.$$

Subtracting the same number also preserves order because it adds an opposite. Geometrically, both values shift by the same distance on the [[Number Line]], so neither passes the other. This property allows constant terms to be removed while solving a [[Linear Inequality in One Variable]].

Development
For many years, a large number of software titles—including games—tended to be
developed using what is commonly known as the waterfall method of development.
Using the waterfall method, a small preproduction team would define the entire
project via a massive game design document that the production team was expected
to follow exactly as they developed the game. Using this waterfall approach often
led to games that were not tested until they neared completion, and members of these
production teams could feel more like cogs in a massive machine than actual game
developers.
With the experience you've now gained through paper and digital prototyping in this
book, I'm sure you can immediately see some issues with this approach. In 2001, the
developers who formed the Agile Alliance saw these issues as well, leading to their
Manifesto for Agile Software Development,
1
which reads as follows:
We are uncovering better ways of developing software by doing it and helping
others do it. Through this work we have come to value:
■ Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
■ Working software over comprehensive documentation
■ Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
■ Responding to change over following a plan
That is, while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left
more.
Embedded in these four core values, you can see many of the principles that I've tried to
impress upon you throughout this book:
■ Following your individual design sense, continually asking questions, and
developing an understanding of procedural thinking are more important
than following predefined rules or using a specific development framework.
■ Making a simple prototype that works and iterating on it until it's fun
is more successful than waiting for months until you have the perfect game idea or
solution to your problem.

THE ANATOMY OF A BÉZIER CURVE
Before you go headlong into making all manner of cool things with Bézier curves, it’s worth
taking a moment to understand the parts of a curve. There are three parts to a curve:
• Control points: The control points define the shape of the curve. They’re like verti -
ces in mesh objects. On Bézier curves, the curve always intersects a control point.
• Control point handles: Every control point has a pair of handles that you can use
to control the rotation of that control point.
• Curve segments: Between two control points is a segment that’s mathematically
defined by the location and rotation of the control points.
In its simplest form, a complete curve consists of two control points and a segment
between them. And unlike meshes, curves don’t “fork.” A control point can have at most
one segment going into it and one segment going out of it. There’s no such thing as a
control point that connects three or more segments.

In xUnit, tests are methods decorated with either with the [Fact] or with the [Theory]
attributes. Tests are automatically discovered by the test runner that lists all of them in the
user interface so the user can run either all of them or just a selection of them.
A new instance of the test class is created before running each test, so the test
preparation code contained in the class constructor is executed before each test of the class. If
you also need tear-down code, the test class must implement the IDisposable interface so
that the tear-down code can be included in the IDisposable.Dispose method.
The test code invokes the methods to be tested and then tests the results with methods of

and Assert.NotEmpty(IEnumerable x). There are also methods that verify if a call
throws an exception of a specific type, for instance:

The application layer coordinates a use case around an isolated [[Domain Model]]. It receives a [[Public API Contract]] or message, obtains the required aggregate or services, invokes domain behavior, and persists the resulting changes. It can implement infrastructure-facing interfaces declared by the domain, but it should not reimplement [[Entity Invariant]]s. The layer is an outer boundary: it translates between delivery mechanisms and the domain while keeping business decisions in domain objects.

The application must still create and connect its concrete objects. [[.NET Dependency Injection and Service Lifetimes]] moves that work to a composition boundary. Dependency inversion says high-level behavior should depend on stable abstractions rather than construction details; dependency injection is one way to supply the concrete implementations. The .NET service collection records mappings and lifetimes, and the service provider resolves them when needed. Transient instances are created on demand, scoped instances are shared within a defined boundary such as a web request, and singleton instances are shared across a provider. An implementation factory handles construction that needs explicit logic. These lifetimes do not make mutable code safe: a singleton used from several requests can still suffer races, and building a second service provider does not preserve the first provider's singleton identity.

[[Functional Programming in C Sharp]] offers another way to control complexity. A pure function returns the same result for the same inputs without changing external state, so it is easier to test and reason about. Referential transparency allows a call to be replaced by its value without altering a program's meaning. First-class and higher-order functions turn behavior into a value that can be passed, returned, or stored. C# delegates, lambdas, predicates, and LINQ make this style practical within an object-oriented language. A filtering function can receive its criterion as a function, which is a functional form of the strategy pattern. The design trade-off is to keep stateful I/O and mutation visible at the edges while making the central calculation as explicit as possible.

[[Reactive Programming in .NET]] extends composition from functions over fixed inputs to streams of values arriving over time. A stream can emit values, signal failure, or complete. Subscribers respond to notifications rather than repeatedly polling for changes. Streams can be merged, filtered, and mapped into other streams, allowing event-driven behavior to be described as transformations. The .NET `IObservable<T>` and `IObserver<T>` interfaces describe the provider-consumer contract, while Reactive Extensions supply operators for composing streams. A reactive system is a related but broader architectural idea: responsiveness, resilience, elasticity, and message-driven boundaries concern the behavior of the whole service, not simply the syntax of one observable pipeline.

At the persistence boundary, [[CQRS and Ledger Data Architecture]] separates recording a change from retrieving a view of current state. Online transaction processing favors efficient writes of operational changes; online analytical processing favors reading and aggregating historical information. A ledger-style table records each transaction as a new row, making corrections additional events instead of destructive edits. Summing the entire ledger on every request can become expensive, so a materialized or projected read model provides a faster view. Command Query Responsibility Segregation gives commands and queries distinct models, handlers, and potentially distinct data stores. That separation can support independent scaling and team ownership, but it also introduces synchronization delays: a successful write may not appear in the read model immediately. The pattern is therefore most useful when its read/write asymmetry and audit needs justify the consistency and operational cost.

The application security layer protects the programs through which users and systems process data. It includes secure design, input handling, identity and permission checks, testing, and maintenance throughout the [[Secure Software Development Lifecycle]].

Application weaknesses may expose data even when networks and hosts are well defended. [[Security Code Review]], [[Security Architecture Analysis]], and [[Penetration Testing]] examine different aspects of this layer before and after deployment.

The Auditory Pathway
Our ears are paired sensory organs enabling us to communicate and experience a broad spec-
trum of stimuli generated by our surroundings. This process of transforming variations in air
pressure into a stream of electrical impulses to be analyzed and interpreted by the brain is one
of the most fascinating sensory processes in the entire human body and actually begins outside
of the head. In this section we will examine the mechanics of our sense of hearing by progress-

where electrical impulses are sent onto the audio centers of the brain.
The Outer Ear
Our sense of hearing is enabled through a process known as auditory transduction, within which
one source of stimuli (sound waves) is converted into another (electrical impulses destined for the
brain). As shown in Figure 7.4, key aspects of this process begin when sound waves first reach the
external portion of our ear known as the auricle or pinna (Latin for wing —plural form: pinnea).

The Middle Ear
The auditory canal terminates at a thin, semi-transparent, oval-shaped membrane
approximately 10 mm in diameter called the eardrum (tympanic membrane). Mounted on
an angle between 45 ° and 60 ° in relation to the base of the auditory canal, the eardrum is
stretched by means of a series of small muscles around its perimeter (Gray, 1918; Stinson and
Lawton, 1989). The eardrum is the first of a series of structures in the middle ear that convert
sound waves entering the auditory canal into vibrations in the fluid-filled cochlea.
In a process known as transduction, when sound waves cause the eardrum to vibrate, a series
of three small bones—the malleus, incus, and stapes (also known as the hammer, anvil, and
stirrup and collectively referred to as “ossicles”)—transfer these vibrations across the inner ear.
The first of these small bones, the malleus (or hammer), is securely attached to the back side
of the eardrum, as shown in Figure 7.5. When the eardrum vibrates, the malleus moves in sync.
These vibrations are then passed to the incus and to the stapes. The footplate of the stapes
bone is itself connected to a membrane covering an opening leading into the inner ear known
as the oval window.

switches or networking equipment in most cases. You set up the NLB configuration from inside the
Windows Server tools, and it handles the rest. A downside to unicast is that, because the same MAC
address exists on all NLB server nodes, it causes some intra-node communication problems. In other
words, the servers that are enabled for NLB will have trouble communicating with each other’s IP
addresses. Often, this doesn’t really matter because WEB1 would rarely have reason to communicate

directly with WEB2. But if you really need those web servers to be able to talk with each other consis -
tently and reliably, the easiest solution is to install a separate NIC on each of those servers and use that
NIC for those intra-array communications, while leaving the primary NICs configured for NLB traffic.
The other downside to unicast is that it can create some switch flooding. The switches are unable to
learn a permanent route for the virtual MAC address because we need it to be delivered to all of the
nodes in our array. Since every packet moving to the virtual MAC is being sent down all avenues of
a switch so that it can hit all of the NICs where it needs to be delivered, it has the potential to over -
whelm the switches with this flood of network packets. If you are concerned about that or are getting
complaints from your networking people about switch flooding, you might want to check out one of
the multicast modes for your NLB cluster.

The binomial distribution gives the probability of observing a specified number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials when every trial has the same success probability. Its parameters are the trial count and the per-trial probability.

It models biological counts such as variant-supporting reads when the trials and probability assumptions are appropriate. With many trials and a moderate expected count it approaches a normal shape, while rare events motivate a [[Rare Event Poisson Approximation]].

The Biot-Savart law gives the magnetic field contribution from a current element:

$$dB=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\ell\times\hat r}{r^2}.$$

Integrating along the conductor produces the total field. The cross product fixes direction through the right-hand rule, while geometry determines how contributions reinforce or cancel.

The Bisect tool cuts selected mesh geometry with a user-defined plane. It can retain both sides, clear one side, and optionally fill the cut, making it useful for trimming a model or producing a clean planar division.

The bisection method finds a root of a continuous function on an interval whose endpoints have opposite signs. It repeatedly halves the interval and keeps the half that still brackets a sign change.

The method converges reliably under its assumptions and has a predictable error bound based on interval width. Its convergence is slower than derivative-based methods but does not require a derivative.

The book gives dynamic and kinematic viscosity separate conversion categories because their unit dimensions differ. Dynamic viscosity is represented by centipoise or millipascal seconds, while kinematic viscosity is represented by centistokes or square millimeters per second. Its examples happen to have a factor of one between the listed pairs, but that numerical coincidence does not make the two kinds of viscosity interchangeable. The unit expression identifies which conversion category and target unit are appropriate. See [[Algebraic SI Derived Units]].

Dynamic viscosity also measures a fluid's resistance to shear: a larger shear stress is required to maintain the same velocity gradient in a more viscous fluid. Kinematic viscosity divides dynamic viscosity by density, so it describes momentum diffusion rather than shear resistance alone.

Their unit symbols provide the building blocks for the expressions of derived units. A base unit is not simply a commonly used unit; it is part of this chosen foundation. The book maps collections of dream reports and their words into a full Euclidean correspondence-analysis factor space, then counts approximately ultrametric triangles among text-unit locations. In its case studies, dream reports show a higher measured tendency than several literary and technical text collections.

The coefficient is sensitive to corpus selection, text segmentation, word encoding, dimensionality, and the angular rule used to count triangles. It characterizes relationships in written reports after conscious narration; it is not a direct measurement of the dreamer's unconscious neural activity.

The book measures inherent ultrametricity by examining triples of points before imposing a clustering tree. In a Euclidean embedding, a triple is counted when its triangle is approximately equilateral or isosceles with a small base; the coefficient is the proportion of counted, nondegenerate triples.

Its implementation samples triples when exhaustive enumeration is too costly and uses a chosen angular tolerance, so the value depends on both the embedding and approximation rule. It can compare datasets or encodings for hierarchical tendency without assuming that a particular linkage algorithm's fitted dendrogram is the ground truth.
